title: A Sikh prime minister
hook: a soft-spoken Sikh economist leads India as prime minister

segments.voice: Yesterday, kar seva, and your line was hands build it. Today, service of a very different size: a whole country's government.

On a television screen, a man in a pale blue turban reads a speech. He doesn't shout or wave his arms. His voice is so soft that people lean toward the set to hear him. He's an economist, a man of reports, tables and budgets, and he has just become prime minister of India. His given name is Manmohan, and he carries the name Singh, as Sikh men do. The country comes to know him as Dr. Singh. Today: a Sikh prime minister.
screen: `A PALE BLUE TURBAN ON TELEVISION.` → `A SOFT VOICE, NO SHOUTING.` → `A SIKH PRIME MINISTER.`

segments.voice: First, the road there. Dr. Singh didn't come up through rallies. He was a scholar of economics who worked in government offices for years, and served as finance minister before he led the country. His public biography reads like a list of desks, not a list of speeches. Second, what people saw: a turbaned Sikh at the head of India's government, wearing his faith openly, in the same country this path has followed through some of its hardest years. Some Sikhs, and others, spoke of it as a moment worth noticing. Third, the manner. He was known for a quiet, careful style, and for listening more than he spoke. People argued about his policies, as they argue about every leader's, and this lesson takes no side on them. The thing to notice is the tone. At Ang 470 of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak says that sweetness and humility are the essence of all virtues. Not loudness, not winning the room. Fourth, the everyday version. Most quiet service never reaches a television: a clerk who checks your form twice so it won't be rejected, a nurse on a night shift, a city planner you only notice when the bus comes on time. Sikhs speak of seva as service that doesn't ask to be seen, and it can happen at a desk as well as in a langar hall.
screen: `A LIST OF DESKS, NOT SPEECHES.` · `A TURBAN AT THE HEAD OF GOVERNMENT.` · `SWEETNESS AND HUMILITY.` · `SERVICE AT A DESK.` · then, large: `QUIET SERVICE.`

segments.voice: Think back over a week of errands and appointments, the post office, a school office, the clinic, the road crew, and find one person who did their part well and quietly, never asking to be seen. Hold them in mind for a few breaths; you don't need to know their name. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out, with them in mind.
Nimrata. Humility, the quiet, careful style Dr. Singh showed as India's soft-spoken, turbaned prime minister. Today's word.
Your line: quiet service. Sweetness and humility fit at any desk, anywhere. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Sikhs serve in public office in India and elsewhere while keeping the turban and the articles of faith; in the tradition, service done well and without seeking credit is counted as seva.

chat.says: Why did that Sikh prime minister speak so softly? Aren't leaders supposed to be loud?
options: That's nimrata: Guru Nanak calls sweetness and humility the essence of all virtues.
Sikh custom forbids raising your voice in any speech, so he had no choice.
Soft speech was a campaign trick to win over voters who disliked loud rallies.
chat.meaning: At Ang 470 Guru Nanak names sweetness and humility the essence of virtues; Dr. Singh's quiet, careful manner showed that tone.
